content: To ensure proper functionality, it is essential to save both do-files in the same folder so that they remain linked. You do not need to open the secondary file directly. Preliminary Steps Before Running the Do-File: 1. Adjust Model Settings: Before executing the do-file, modify the model settings to align with your dataset and the type of analysis you intend to perform. This includes changing values, alarm/outbreak thresholds, and other parameters. These adjustments will enhance the accuracy of outbreak predictions. 2. Locate Settings in the Do-File: Figures 4-9 in the guide illustrate where these settings can be found in the do-file, enabling you to make the necessary changes. 3. Use Line Numbers for Reference: Each line of code in the do-file is numbered. Use these line numbers to identify where to make changes as per the instructions. Running the Do-File and Data Calibration: Starting Point (Line 15): Choose the folder where your results and outputs will be saved. Create a folder on your desktop named Stata Analysis, copy its file path, and insert it between the quotation marks in the do-file. This ensures all results and analyses are stored in this folder. Dataset Identification (Line 21): Specify the name of the Excel sheet containing your records. For example, if the sheet is named Sheet1, enter this name in the do-file so Stata can locate your dataset. Dividing the Dataset (Line 29): To detect alarm indicators for outbreak prediction, divide your dataset into two time periods: a historic/run-in period and an evaluation period. Specify the end date of the run-in period (e.g., 201326 for year 2013, week 26). Stata will automatically use data after this date for evaluation. Analysis Type (Line 34): Choose between retrospective analysis (result = 0) to identify alarm indicators or prospective early warning system generation (result = 1). Always run the retrospective analysis first to calibrate settings and identify alarm indicators before proceeding to the early warning system. District Selection (Line 38): Specify the district codes for analysis. Leave this field blank to analyze all districts or enter multiple district codes separated by spaces. Adjusting Outbreak Indicator Settings: Population Definition (Line 46): Define the annual population for each district. For example, if the column in your dataset is labeled population, enter this label in the do-file. Case Labeling (Line 48): Specify the column name for incident case data, such as weekly_hospitalised_cases. Ensure the name matches the column title in your dataset. Outbreak Period Definition (Line 52): Define the minimum number of consecutive weeks required to classify an outbreak. For instance, setting outbreak_period_length = 3 means at least three consecutive weeks are needed to define an outbreak. Calibrating Alarm Indicators: Alarm Indicator Selection (Line 58): Choose the alarm indicators to test for predictive capacity, such as weekly_average_temperature or weekly_total_rainfall. Ensure your dataset is complete, as missing data can negatively impact results. Window Size for Alarm Indicators (Line 61): Specify the time period (in weeks) over which alarm indicator values are averaged. For example, setting alarm_window = 3 calculates the mean value over the current week and the two preceding weeks. Graphical and Advanced Settings: Graphical Outputs (Line 72): Generate graphs for specific districts or all districts. For example, setting graph_per_district = 15 will create graphs for district 15 only. Multiple district codes can be entered, separated by spaces. Seasonal Variation (Line 79): If certain alarm indicators are better predictors at specific times of the year, divide the year into periods. For example, setting season_length = 4 divides the year into 4-week intervals for analysis. Outbreak Threshold Adjustment (Line 86): Define the window size for calculating outbreak proportions. For example, setting outbreak_window = 4 calculates the proportion over four consecutive outbreak periods. Adjust this value based on your dataset and evaluation criteria. Spline Application (Line 98): Choose whether to apply a spline function to model the relationship between alarm indicators and dengue cases. Set spline = 1 for a monotonic relationship or spline = 0 for a non-monotonic relationship. Interpreting Results: Output Tables: After running the do-file, two tables will be displayed in Stata: 1. Absolute Values: Includes metrics such as outbreak weeks, outbreak periods, total alarms, correct alarms, false alarms, missed outbreaks, and defined outbreaks. These values reflect the success or failure of the parameters used in the analysis. 2. Proportions: Displays sensitivity (percentage of outbreaks correctly predicted) and positive predictive value (PPV, percentage of alarms that correctly predicted outbreaks). Aim for sensitivity and PPV values as close to 100% as possible. Operational Perspective: For example, if sensitivity is 60%, the system correctly detects 6 out of 10 outbreaks but misses 4. If PPV is 70%, 7 out of 10 alarms are correct, while 3 are false. Adjust parameters such as the z-value and alarm threshold to optimize these metrics. Final Steps: Once all changes are made, run the do-file to generate results. Use retrospective data to build and refine the early warning system, ensuring it provides accurate and actionable predictions for dengue outbreaks.
